questions.q: Write the complete symbol (ᴬᶻX) for an atom with 17 protons, 18 neutrons, and 17 electrons. Identify the element name.
questions.a: Answer: ³⁵₁₇Cl (Chlorine-35). Z = 17 (protons), A = 17 + 18 = 35. A wrong answer like ³⁵₁₈Ar reveals confusion between atomic number and mass number, or inability to identify element from Z. Writing ¹⁷₃⁵Cl shows misunderstanding of notation convention (superscript = mass number, subscript = atomic number).

questions.q: Explain why ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl have identical chemical properties but different densities and rates of diffusion.
questions.a: Chemical properties depend on electron configuration (17 electrons, same arrangement). Physical properties like density (mass/volume) and diffusion rate (Graham's law: rate ∝ 1/√M) depend on nuclear mass. A wrong answer citing "different valence electrons" reveals confusion between isotopes and isobars, or misunderstanding that neutrons don't affect electron cloud.

questions.q: A sample of element X has two isotopes: ⁶³X (69% abundance) and ⁶⁵X (31% abundance). Calculate the average atomic mass of X. Identify X from the periodic table.
questions.a: Average mass = (63 × 0.69) + (65 × 0.31) = 43.47 + 20.15 = 63.62 u ≈ 63.5 u. Element is Copper (Cu, Z=29). A wrong answer of 64 u (simple average) reveals misunderstanding of weighted average. Identifying Zn (Z=30) shows inability to link atomic number to periodic table position.

questions.q: Compare the species: ⁴⁰₁₈Ar, ⁴⁰₂₀Ca, ³⁹₁₉K⁺. Which are isobars? Which are isoelectronic? Justify using subatomic particle counts.
questions.a: Isobars: ⁴⁰₁₈Ar and ⁴⁰₂₀Ca (same A=40, different Z). Isoelectronic: ⁴⁰₁₈Ar (18e⁻), ⁴⁰₂₀Ca²⁺ (18e⁻), ³⁹₁₉K⁺ (18e⁻) - all have 18 electrons. A wrong answer pairing Ar and K⁺ as isobars reveals confusion between mass number and electron count. Missing Ca²⁺ shows inability to calculate electrons in ions.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Since ¹⁴₆C and ¹⁴₇N are isobars, they have similar chemical reactivity." Is it correct? Explain.
questions.a: Incorrect. Isobars have different Z (6 vs 7), hence different electron configurations (C: 2,4; N: 2,5) and valencies. Chemical reactivity depends on electrons, not total nucleons. A student agreeing reveals the misconception that "same mass number = same properties", confusing isobars with isotopes.

questions.q: Design a method to separate ²³⁵U and ²³⁸U isotopes for nuclear fuel enrichment. Explain why chemical separation fails and what physical property you would exploit.
questions.a: Chemical separation fails because isotopes have identical electron configurations. Exploit mass difference (3 u) via gaseous diffusion or gas centrifugation of UF₆ - lighter ²³⁵UF₆ diffuses/centrifuges slightly faster. A poor answer suggesting fractional distillation or precipitation shows ignorance of identical chemical behaviour and the tiny mass difference requiring specialized physical methods.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Isotopes are atoms of the same element having ______ atomic number (Z) but different mass numbers (A) due to varying numbers of neutrons in the nucleus; isobars are atoms of different elements having the same mass number (A) but different atomic numbers (Z).
Fill in the blank: Observe a chlorine gas cylinder label showing "Cl = 35.5 u" - how can an element have a ______ atomic mass?
What is Isotopes? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Isotopes are atoms of the same element having identical atomic number (Z) but different mass numbers (A) due to varying numbers of neutrons in the nucleus; isobars are atoms of different elements having the same mass number (A) but different atomic numbers (Z).

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Isotopes?
questions.a: Students write isotopic notation as ¹⁷₃⁵Cl (swapping superscript/subscript) and calculate neutrons as Z - A instead of A - Z.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can calculate protons, neutrons, and electrons for any given isotope/isobar notation (e.g., ³⁵₁₇Cl, ³⁷₁₇Cl, ⁴⁰₁₈Ar, ⁴⁰₂₀Ca), explain why isotopes show identical chemical properties but different physical properties, and apply the (n + l) rule to predict relative stability of isotopes in nuclear chemistry contexts.
